title: What does Wythenshawe mean to the people who know it best?

input.lead: As Wythenshawe marks its centenary, 100 people tell the BBC what it is really like to live and work there
input.summary: As Wythenshawe marks its centenary, 100 people tell the BBC what it is really like to live and work there
input.evidence_text: This year marks 100 years since Wythenshawe Hall was donated to Manchester Corporation At the time, the city was in urgent need of more housing In 1920 an urban planner called Patrick Abercrombie identified Wythenshawe as the only undeveloped land suitable for building a housing estate close to Manchester To turn his proposal into a reality, Ernest and Shena Simon bought Wythenshawe Hall from Robert Henry Grenville Tatton in 1926, which they donated to the city's corporation (now known as the council) The idea was that people could be rehoused away from industrial Manchester into what became known as the "Garden City" To celebrate 100 years, BBC North West Tonight has spoken to 100 people from the area about what Wythenshawe means to them

title: Wythenshawe 100: Cabaret club on Europe's biggest council estate

input.lead: The Golden Garter opened its doors in the Wythenshawe area of Manchester in 1968 and attracted huge stars
input.summary: The Golden Garter opened its doors in the Wythenshawe area of Manchester in 1968 and attracted huge stars
input.evidence_text: Wythenshawe 100: Cabaret club on Europe's biggest council estate - BBC News Image source, John Orchard Image caption, The Golden Garter in Wythenshawe proved to be a popular venue when it opened in 1968 By Kaya Black and Lauren Hirst , North West Published 1 hour ago When the Golden Garter cabaret club opened its doors for the first time in October 1968, TV legend Sir Bruce Forsyth was the first name on the door. Situated on a council estate in the Wythenshawe area of Manchester, people travelled from far and wide to enjoy shows at the 1,400-capacity venue. From music stars Dusty Springfield, Roy Orbison and Eartha Kitt to comedians Tommy Cooper and Ronnie Corbett, there was never a shortage of acts wanting to appear. "I think Dusty Springfield was the big highlight for me," said 79-year-old John Orchard, who was a pianist for Shep's Banjo Boys from 1969 to 1972. "She was my favourite singer in the 1960s and all of a sudden there she is at the Golden Garter. "This is a nightclub in Wythenshawe under the flight path of the Ringway airport (now known as Manchester Airport) in the middle of the biggest council estate in Europe. "So it was a bit incongruous, but it was a fantastic place and Wythenshawe loved it and it loved Wythenshawe." Image source, Unknown Image caption, The Golden Garter could pack in crowds of up to 1,400 The Golden Garter holds many happy memories for Paul Stoloff, who was a bassist for the Golden Garter Showband from 1970 to 1982. "It was good fun - happy times," he said. "It was interesting because it was different music every week. "So if you didn't like what they're doing, it'd be different for the next week." title: Motorcyclist killed by vehicle on M56 after police pursuit

input.lead: The man was spotted driving dangerously by officers on the M60 near Stockport Pyramid, police say
input.summary: The man was spotted driving dangerously by officers on the M60 near Stockport Pyramid, police say
input.evidence_text: Motorcyclist killed by vehicle on M56 after police pursuit - BBC News Image source, Press Association Image caption, Greater Manchester Police is appealing for information Published 18 October 2026 A motorcycle rider being pursued by police on a motorway has been killed after he fled his bike and was hit by another vehicle. Officers spotted a red motorcycle being driven in a dangerous manner on the M60 clockwise around Stockport Pyramid shortly before 19:30 BST on Saturday, Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said. The force said it was brought to a stop on the M56 but the man ran off across the motorway and was hit and killed by another vehicle. GMP said, in line with procedures following a fatality after police contact, it has referred the matter to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC). The motorcycle had been posing a significant risk to members of the public using the motorway, the force said. "Tactical contact" was made with the bike at low speed on the hard shoulder by junction 5 near Manchester Airport and it was brought to a stop between junctions 3 and 4 of the M56 near Wythenshawe, it said. The rider was given emergency medical treatment by an ambulance crew but he was pronounced dead at the scene. A second man, who was not involved in the initial pursuit, was arrested at the scene on suspicion of causing death by careless driving when under the influence of drink or drugs and causing death by driving uninsured. The incident resulted in the closure of part of the M56 overnight. GMP has referred the matter to the IOPC which has decided an independent investigation is required. title: Hindley couple spent 20 years building railway station garden

input.lead: Sheila and Sandy Davidson have been planting trees, flowers and shrubs at Hindley station for 20 years
input.summary: Sheila and Sandy Davidson have been planting trees, flowers and shrubs at Hindley station for 20 years
input.evidence_text: Hindley couple spent 20 years building railway station garden - BBC News Image caption, The community garden has been created beside both platforms at Hindley station in Wigan By Richard Stead North West Published 18 October 2026 A couple who have spent 20 years building a community garden at their local railway station have said they hope it will be named as the Best in Britain. Hindley Station in Wigan has been nominated in an annual "World Cup" of stations competition run by train operating companies. Sheila and Sandy Davidson have been planting trees, flowers and shrubs alongside the platforms for two decades. "We just came down almost 20 years ago and decided to plant a few bulbs on the Manchester-bound platform," said 80-year-old Sheila from the Friends of Hindley Station. "Everybody in the area is wonderful, they all support us and we get so much help from people on social media who donate things for the garden." Image caption, Sheila Davidson is the Friends of Hindley Station's lead volunteer Sheila added: "It's putting Hindley on the map, so to even get in the World Cup of stations is such an honour, but we really would like to win." The Rail Delivery Group, which represents train operating companies, organises the competition every year, with passengers voting for the winner. Ashington railway station in Northumberland won the award last year after passenger services returned to the town in 2024 following an absence of 60 years. Image caption, The platforms at Hindley Station have been turned into vibrant community gardens and allotments Hindley station opened in 1848 and is situated between Bolton and Wigan, with regular direct services across the north of England. title: Greater Manchester schools told to urgently improve by inspectors

input.lead: The two primary schools in Stockport and Dukinfield are both placed in special measures
input.summary: The two primary schools in Stockport and Dukinfield are both placed in special measures
input.evidence_text: Greater Manchester schools told to urgently improve by inspectors - BBC News Image source, Press Association Image caption, Ofsted has changed its rating system By Charlotte Hall Local Democracy Reporting Service Published 18 October 2026 Two schools in Greater Manchester have been told they need urgent improvement following Ofsted inspections. St Thomas' Church of England Primary in Stockport has been placed in special measures with inspectors raising concerns about teaching, attendance and leadership. Ravensfield Primary in Dukinfield, already in special measures after staff reported violence towards teachers had reached "untenable levels", had only made minor improvements, inspectors said. The CLIC Trust, which runs Ravensfield, said management "recognised the seriousness of Ofsted's findings" and were committed to "delivering rapid improvements". St Thomas' Primary School has been contacted for comment. The government watchdog found the Stockport school was "failing to provide an acceptable standard of education". It was criticised for leaving pupils "ill-equipped" for the next stage of their education, with a "patchy" knowledge of most subjects. According to the report, too many children were also persistently absent, the Local Democracy Reporting Service , external said. Lead inspector David Spruce found pupils had been "hindered by a range of factors that ultimately stem from ineffective leadership and governance". Weaknesses in curriculum design and teaching practices had not been sufficiently addressed and leaders had not tackled "deep-rooted attendance issues", he said. input.evidence_text: Politics From next month, these two Greater Manchester councils could be acting unlawfully Government planning reforms come into effect on October 31. But the two Greater Manchester councils voted not to accept them Add to preferred sources Comments N Two Greater Manchester planning departments will be acting unlawfully in less than two weeks after rejecting government changes to the way planning applications are approved and denied Councillors in both Tameside and Bolton voted not to accept new measures to implement legally binding changes, which means as things stand, from November 1 their planning committees will not be legally compliant and councillors will have no say on planning matters After that date, if nothing changes, officers will make all planning decisions in the two boroughs, it is understood. However, as the situation is unprecedented the true ramifications of not accepting the new reforms is unknown At recent full council meetings, councillors in Tameside and Bolton were told of the statutory introduction of the national scheme of delegation of planning functions will come into law on October 31, which alters arrangements for determining planning applications across England Under the new rules planning applications would be split into two tiers – Schedule 1 applications and Schedule 2 applications, designated by planning officers. Schedule 1 includes smaller and more technical applications that would only be dealt with by planning officers

Understanding the format helps you judge what is actually being of GIA, the Gemological Institute of America, and IGI, the International Gemological Institute, are grading laboratories. Retailers often refer to these documents as diamond certificates. Check the issuing laboratory and the details on the report itself The lab diamonds UK shoppers compare may have reports from different laboratories. Lily Arkwright, which has a showroom in Didsbury, lists lab-grown diamond rings with GIA or IGI documentation. Ask to see your shortlisted stone’s report before visiting, so you can discuss its det Start by checking the laboratory’s name, the report number and whether the document identifies the diamond as laboratory-grown. Different regions have different strengths, assets and specialisms, and there was a strong view that greater collaboration between places could create bi Procurement and buying local also featured strongly. The discussion highlighted the role public sector buying power can play in supporting regional businesses, helping successful pilots move into commercial contracts and strengthening UK capability in areas such as AI and cyber There was also a broader conversation about sovereignty and the UK’s role internationally. title: Is the funding market getting harder and what could that mean for Manchester? | Manchester Digital

input.lead: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing.
input.summary: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised
input.evidence_text: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised. More capital is being concentrated in fewer companies while the market for exits remains difficult Financial news recently added another dimension to that discussion. AI-related shares fell last week after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slower approach to the development of increasingly capable AI models. Nvidia finished the day down 3.4%, SoftBank fell 10.7% in Tokyo Additionally, the Bank of England is predicted to increase interest rates later this year, which could affect the North West's tech funding landscape by raising the cost of capital across the board, compressing valuations, pushing investors toward profitability over growth-at-all The British Business Bank's 2026 Small Business Equity Tracker found that equity investment into UK smaller businesses fell 4% to £12.3bn in 2025. Seed deal numbers fell 27% and venture deals fell 13%. AI companies attracted 44% of all investment into smaller businesses while the Beauhurst recorded £14.4bn of UK equity investment across 2,799 deals in the first half of 2026 but three AI companies accounted for 29% of all the capital raised. Those very large rounds can make the overall market look stronger than it feels to businesses raising at seed or Ser Beauhurst's analysis shows that UK equity investment more than doubled between 2017 and 2021 to £32.2bn while annual exits remained at around 400 to 500. An exit takes a median of four years from a funding round

input.evidence_text: 43 years on from our only participation in the European Cup – a first-round defeat to Fenerbahce in 1968 – we qualified for the Champions League for the 2011/12 season. Now, as we approach our 150th game in this historic competition when we take on AEK Athens on Tuesday, we can say the Champions League has more than delivered on its guarantee of joy, heartbreak and everything in between. Having qualified for the continent’s hallmark cup competition in every season since Roberto Mancini led us there in 2011, we are currently on the longest ongoing run of appearances in the Champions League of any English side. The level of consistency required not to miss out in all that time speaks volumes to our domestic dominance particularly under Pep Guardiola but also with Mancini and Manuel Pellegrini. We have, after all, won the Premier League more than every other club combined since that 2011/12 season began. However, it’s not always been the same in Europe. With the finest of margins often deciding knockout ties between the most talented players on the planet, it felt for a long time as if City were destined never to lift the famous old trophy with the giant ear-shaped handles. That all changed in 2023, when Rodri curled home against Inter in Istanbul and Ederson produced a last-minute diving save to set the seal on a historic Treble. City had more than deserved it, having swept aside German champions Bayern Munich and defending winners Real Madrid in the previous rounds. But what you deserve isn’t always what you get in the Champions League. Bernardo Silva, who left City in the summer as our joint-most decorated player having been integral to all the successes under Guardiola, said this in his final interview with the club: “I think more of our teams could have done the same.
